```{r}
#| label: config
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

# Include the supplementary sensitivity checks (child document); when FALSE the text says they are not shown
show_sensitivity <- FALSE
sens_ref <- if (show_sensitivity) "[Sensitivity checks](#sec-sensitivity)" else "sensitivity checks not shown"

# Fits from the migrant analysis script (forest-reference variants, 2026-11-15): forest as the reference habitat, one intercept per survey period with the two 2016-17 periods merged (2025-26 reference), team-specific warm-up slopes and the free spatial range prior
fit_dir <- "Derived/Rdata/Model_output/Temporal/Single_species"
# Single-species fits only for migrants detected often enough outside forest to estimate habitat contrasts
species_ss <- c("Setophaga_striata", "Setophaga_ruticilla", "Piranga_rubra")
# Radii of landscape canopy cover carried into the base models (user, 2026-11-15): S. striata's single-species profile minimum and the community's; S. ruticilla and P. rubra without canopy, as no radius was supported for them (user, 2026-11-16)
striata_radius <- 5000
comm_radius <- 3000
# Base models (2026-11-16): the forest-reference variants plus landscape canopy cover at the chosen radius, with an arrival-period indicator in place of day of season (user, 2026-11-16: with period intercepts the linear day-of-season slope came almost only from forest in October-December 2016 vs March 2017); arrival ends 1 December, and the multi-species model has doubled chains (its silvopasture among-species variance mixed poorly at the standard length)
ss_oct15_tags <- c(Setophaga_striata = paste0("oct15_team_day_fref_r", striata_radius, "_arr_free"), Setophaga_ruticilla = "oct15_team_day_fref_arr_free", Piranga_rubra = "oct15_team_day_fref_arr_free")
# Single-species base models on species-specific windows (user, 2026-11-18; the analysis script's swin flag): start from our Meta data (15 October for S. striata, 24 September for S. ruticilla and P. rubra, whose detection then needs teams 1 and 2), arrival end and season end from eBird Status and Trends' non-breeding start and end; the 15 October fits above remain the base of the season-term comparison and the sensitivity checks
ss_tags <- c(Setophaga_striata = paste0("swin_team_day_fref_r", striata_radius, "_arr_free"), Setophaga_ruticilla = "swin_team_day_sep24_fref_arr_free", Piranga_rubra = "swin_team_day_sep24_fref_arr_free")
# Multi-species base model (user, 2026-11-17): season from 24 September, so the passage detections of C. virens and C. ustulatus (GAICA's 2019 distance-gradient surveys) are kept, with a passage indicator (mean date before 15 October) and an arrival indicator ending 15 November; teams 1 and 2 (the distance-gradient surveys) added to detection
ms_tag <- paste0("sep24_team_day_sep24_fref_r", comm_radius, "_arrnov15_pass_free_ig11_long")
# The same 24 September data with shorter chains: passage + arrival ending 1 December, passage + arrival ending 15 November, and arrival ending 1 December alone, for the choice of passage and arrival terms
ms_sep24_test_tags <- c(pass_dec1 = "arr_pass", pass_nov15 = "arrnov15_pass", dec1 = "arr") %>% map_chr(\(x) paste0("sep24_team_day_sep24_fref_r", comm_radius, "_", x, "_free_ig11_short"))
# The multi-species model on the 15 October season with arrival ending 1 December (the earlier base model), for the comparison of season terms on the same data as the fits below
ms_oct15_tag <- paste0("oct15_team_day_fref_r", comm_radius, "_arr_free_ig11_long")
# The same base models with a linear day of season or without any season term, and the multi-species model with arrival ending 1 November, for the comparison of season terms
ss_day_tags <- c(Setophaga_striata = paste0("oct15_team_day_fref_r", striata_radius, "_free"), Setophaga_ruticilla = "oct15_team_day_fref_free", Piranga_rubra = "oct15_team_day_fref_free")
ms_day_tag <- paste0("oct15_team_day_fref_r", comm_radius, "_free_ig11")
ss_noday_tags <- c(Setophaga_striata = paste0("oct15_team_day_fref_r", striata_radius, "_noday_free"), Setophaga_ruticilla = "oct15_team_day_fref_noday_free", Piranga_rubra = "oct15_team_day_fref_noday_free")
ms_noday_tag <- paste0("oct15_team_day_fref_r", comm_radius, "_noday_free_ig11")
ms_arrnov_tag <- paste0("oct15_team_day_fref_r", comm_radius, "_arrnov_free_ig11_long")
# S. striata without canopy (with the arrival indicator), for the WAIC of its canopy ring in the base model
striata_nc_arr_tag <- "oct15_team_day_fref_arr_free"
# The same models without canopy and with day of season, the base of the sensitivity variants below (habitat-by-rainfall, prior variance, reference level, silvopasture's distance slope, silvopasture split), which were not refit (user, 2026-11-16: sensitivity checks are rerun before publication)
ss_tag <- "oct15_team_day_fref_free"
ms_nc_tag <- "oct15_team_day_fref_free_ig11"
# Habitat-by-annual-rainfall interaction (user, 2026-11-19): multi-species only, on the community base model without pasture (nopast flag: a pasture rainfall slope would rest on a handful of detections), so habitat is forest vs silvopasture; the single-species models stay additive
ms_rain_tag <- paste0("nopast_sep24_team_day_sep24_fref_r", comm_radius, "_rain_arrnov15_pass_free_ig11_long")
# Prior sensitivity: variance of the normal prior on the occupancy coefficients (single-species) or on their community-level means (multi-species), 1 and 10 instead of spOccupancy's default 2.72
prior_vars <- c(1, 10)
# Scale of effect of landscape canopy cover (2026-11-15): ring profiles and spatial-effect summaries, written by the migrant analysis script's ring_compare section
ring_csv <- "Derived/Excels/Migrant_ss_ring_comparison.csv"
ring_loadings_csv <- "Derived/Excels/Migrant_ms_ring_spatial_loadings.csv"
# Non-spatial check of the community radius (2026-11-15 night): location random effect in place of the spatial factor, with and without canopy
ms_nonsp_tag <- "oct15_team_day_fref_nonsp_ig11"
ms_ring_nonsp_tag <- paste0("oct15_team_day_fref_r", comm_radius, "_nonsp_ig11")
# Migrants outside Meta (user, 2026-11-16): in-season point counts from all ecoregions in the sibling wrangling repository, and AVONET long-distance migrants from its trait table
wrangling_dir <- "../Ssp-bird-data-wrangling/Derived/Excels/"
# AVONET long-distance migrants that are not Nearctic-Neotropical migrants in Colombia (resident or austral-migrant populations, or breeding only in Middle America), excluded as for the Meta migrant list
not_nearctic <- c("Chrysolampis mosquitus", "Coccyzus lansbergi", "Elaenia pallatangae", "Empidonomus varius", "Falco sparverius", "Myiodynastes maculatus", "Myiopagis viridicata", "Pyrocephalus rubinus", "Tyrannus savana", "Vireo flavoviridis")
# Species whose Colombian records may include resident populations (marked in the table)
mixed_status <- c("Setophaga petechia", "Vireo olivaceus")
# The tag must be followed directly by the fit date, so e.g. "fref_free" does not also match "fref_free_short"
fit_path <- \(sp, tag) list.files(fit_dir, paste0("^Occ_mod_", sp, "_", tag, "_\\d{4}-\\d{2}-\\d{2}\\.rds$"), full.names = TRUE)
stopifnot(all(map_lgl(list(ss_tags, ss_oct15_tags), \(tags) all(imap_int(tags, \(tag, sp) length(fit_path(sp, tag))) == 1))),all(map_int(c(ss_tag, striata_nc_arr_tag), \(tag) length(fit_path("Setophaga_striata", tag))) == 1), all(map_int(c(ms_tag, ms_rain_tag, ms_oct15_tag, ms_sep24_test_tags, ms_day_tag, ms_nc_tag, ms_nonsp_tag, ms_ring_nonsp_tag), \(tag) length(fit_path("10_boreal_migrants", tag))) == 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: summaries
## Species coefficients with the single-species names: single-species fits, each migrant's coefficients from the multi-species fit, and the community means
ss_beta <- map(fits, \(m) m$beta.samples)
species_beta <- \(m) map(set_names(Migrants), \(sp) {
  b <- as.matrix(m$beta.samples)[, str_ends(colnames(m$beta.samples), paste0("-", sp)), drop = FALSE]
  colnames(b) <- str_remove(colnames(b), paste0("-", sp, "$"))
  b
})
ms_beta <- species_beta(ms_fit)
comm_beta <- as.matrix(ms_fit$beta.comm.samples)
## Habitat contrasts on the logit scale (forest is the reference level; they do not depend on the other covariates in the additive model)
contrasts_of <- \(b) list(`Silvopasture vs pasture` = b[, "Habitat_frefSsp"] - b[, "Habitat_frefPastizales"], `Forest vs pasture` = -b[, "Habitat_frefPastizales"], `Silvopasture vs forest` = b[, "Habitat_frefSsp"])
ss_contrasts <- map(ss_beta, contrasts_of)
ms_contrasts <- map(ms_beta, contrasts_of)
comm_contrasts <- contrasts_of(comm_beta)
striata_nc_contrasts <- contrasts_of(striata_nc$beta.samples)
## Largest change in a habitat contrast (posterior medians, logit scale) between the 15 October and 24 September multi-species fits, for S. striata and the community-level means
max_shift <- \(a, b) max(abs(map_dbl(a, median) - map_dbl(b, median)))
passage_shift <- c(striata = max_shift(ms_contrasts$Setophaga_striata, contrasts_of(species_beta(ms_oct15)$Setophaga_striata)), comm = max_shift(comm_contrasts, contrasts_of(as.matrix(ms_oct15$beta.comm.samples))))
rm(ms_oct15)
## Convergence: largest Rhat of the single-species fits, community-level Rhat of the multi-species fit and its species coefficients above 1.1
max_rhat_ss <- max(map_dbl(fits, \(m) max(unlist(m$rhat), na.rm = TRUE)))
max_rhat_comm <- max(unlist(ms_fit$rhat[c("beta.comm", "alpha.comm", "tau.sq.beta", "tau.sq.alpha")]), na.rm = TRUE)
# Largest community-level Rhat among the occupancy terms; the text says the overall maximum is a detection term
max_rhat_comm_occ <- max(unlist(ms_fit$rhat[c("beta.comm", "tau.sq.beta")]), na.rm = TRUE)
stopifnot(max_rhat_comm > max_rhat_comm_occ)
## Effective range of the shared spatial factor (km; exponential correlation, 3 / phi)
eff_range_km <- 3 / ms_fit$theta.samples[, grep("phi", colnames(ms_fit$theta.samples))[1]] / 1000
n_sp_rhat <- sum(unlist(ms_fit$rhat[c("beta", "alpha")]) > 1.1, na.rm = TRUE)

## Prediction conditions: the reference period (2025-26, surveyed in all three habitats), at its mean day of season for the sensitivity fits that still include it, at the forest edge, other covariates at their means, spatial random effect at zero (an average location)
ref_col <- which(Periods_kept == Period_ref)
day_ref <- mean(ss_l$occ.covs$Day_season[surveyed_lp[, ref_col], ref_col])
hab_labels <- c(Pastizales = "Pasture", Ssp = "Silvopasture", Bosque = "Forest")
hab_colors <- c(Pasture = "#eda100", Silvopasture = "#6250d6", Forest = "#008300")
## Occupancy draws for one habitat; distances in SD units, silvopasture cover and day of season (fits that include it) on the model's standardized scales
pred_occ <- function(b, hab, dist_open = 0, dist_inside = 0, ssp = 0, day = day_ref, prec = 0, canopy = 0) {
  eta <- b[, "(Intercept)"] + b[, "Dist_open"] * dist_open + b[, "Dist_inside"] * dist_inside + b[, "ssp"] * ssp + b[, "Tot_prec"] * prec
  if ("Day_season" %in% colnames(b)) eta <- eta + b[, "Day_season"] * day
  # Fits with landscape canopy cover (one ring), standardized over that ring
  canopy_term <- grep("^Canopy_r", colnames(b), value = TRUE)
  if (length(canopy_term)) eta <- eta + b[, canopy_term] * canopy
  if (hab != "Bosque") eta <- eta + b[, paste0("Habitat_fref", hab)]
  # Habitat-by-rainfall and habitat-by-cover fits: the habitat's difference from the forest slope
  int_values <- c(Tot_prec = prec, ssp = ssp)
  for (k in names(int_values)) {
    int_col <- paste0("Habitat_fref", hab, ":", k)
    if (int_col %in% colnames(b)) eta <- eta + b[, int_col] * int_values[[k]]
  }
  plogis(eta)
}
## Occupancy draws at one value of one covariate, given in display units (m: signed distance to the forest edge; ssp: % within 300 m; prec: annual rainfall in mm; canopy: % canopy cover in the community's ring), others at the prediction conditions
pred_at <- function(b, hab_label, var, x) {
  hab <- names(hab_labels)[hab_labels == hab_label]
  switch(var,
    m = pred_occ(b, hab, dist_open = pmax(x, 0) / dist_sd_m, dist_inside = pmax(-x, 0) / dist_sd_m),
    ssp = pred_occ(b, hab, ssp = (x - ssp_scale$Mean) / ssp_scale$SD),
    prec = pred_occ(b, hab, prec = (x - prec_scale$Mean) / prec_scale$SD),
    canopy = pred_occ(b, hab, canopy = (x - canopy_scale$Mean) / canopy_scale$SD))
}
summarise_draws <- \(tbl) tbl %>% mutate(med = map_dbl(draws, median), lcl = map_dbl(draws, quantile, 0.025), ucl = map_dbl(draws, quantile, 0.975)) %>% select(-draws)

## Table formatting shared by all tables: PDF with booktabs rules, alternate row shading, 9 pt and no extra row spacing, species in italics and multi-line headers broken where given ("\n"); Word plain
latex <- knitr::is_latex_output()
italic_species <- \(sp, marks = "") if (latex) paste0("\\textit{", sp, "}", marks) else paste0("*", sp, "*", marks)
star_mark <- if (latex) "*" else "\\*"
report_table <- function(tbl, col_names = names(tbl), align = NULL, widths = NULL) {
  if (!latex) return(kable(tbl, col.names = str_replace_all(col_names, "\n", " "), align = align))
  col_names <- map_chr(col_names, \(x) if (str_detect(x, "\n")) kableExtra::linebreak(x, align = "c") else x)
  out <- kable(tbl, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, linesep = "", align = align, col.names = col_names) %>%
    kableExtra::kable_styling(latex_options = "striped", font_size = 9)
  # Column widths (NA leaves a column at its natural width)
  for (i in which(!is.na(widths))) out <- kableExtra::column_spec(out, i, width = widths[i])
  out
}

## Table 1: visits with a detection (season window) of every migrant in the multi-species model
data_tbl <- tibble(sp = Migrants) %>%
  mutate(Species = italic_species(species_label(sp), if_else(sp %in% species_ss, star_mark, "")), `Visits with a detection` = detections[sp],
         Detected = map_chr(sp, \(s) paste(comm_det_lp_by_habitat[[s]][c("Pastizales", "Ssp", "Bosque")], collapse = " / "))) %>%

## Occupancy by habitat, single-species fits

rare_sp <- setdiff(Migrants, c(species_ss, "Catharus_ustulatus"))
rare_dev <- \(term) map_dbl(set_names(rare_sp), \(sp) median(ms_fit$beta.samples[, paste0(term, "-", sp)]) - median(ms_fit$beta.comm.samples[, term]))
rare_dev_pasture <- rare_dev("Habitat_frefPastizales")
rare_dev_ssp <- rare_dev("Habitat_frefSsp")

## Location-period table per species: habitat, signed distance to the forest edge (m; negative inside forest), silvopasture cover within 300 m (%), day of season, posterior mean latent occupancy (z) and whether the species was detected at any visit (det), for the figure ticks
ssp_pct <- ss_l$occ.covs$ssp * ssp_scale$SD + ssp_scale$Mean
# Covariates from a data list: the default data (15 October window) or a fit's own; habitat and annual rainfall are one value per location, recycled down the period columns
lp_table <- function(z_mean, sp, det = NA, dat = ss_l) {
  oc <- dat$occ.covs
  surveyed <- apply(dat$y, 1:2, \(v) any(!is.na(v)))
  tibble(Species = species_label(sp), Habitat = hab_labels[rep(as.character(oc$Habitat), ncol(surveyed))], m = c(oc$Dist_open - oc$Dist_inside) * dist_sd_m, ssp = c(oc$ssp) * ssp_scale$SD + ssp_scale$Mean, prec = rep(as.numeric(oc$Tot_prec), ncol(surveyed)) * prec_scale$SD + prec_scale$Mean, canopy = c(oc[[paste0("Canopy_r", comm_radius)]]) * canopy_scale$SD + canopy_scale$Mean, day = c(oc$Day_season), z = c(z_mean), det = c(det), surveyed = c(surveyed)) %>%
    filter(surveyed) %>%
    mutate(Habitat = factor(Habitat, hab_labels))
}
lp_of_fits <- \(fit_l, data_l) imap(fit_l, \(fit, sp) lp_table(apply(fit$z.samples, 2:3, mean), sp, apply(fit$y, 1:2, \(v) any(v == 1, na.rm = TRUE)), data_l[[sp]]$ss_l)) %>% list_rbind() %>% mutate(Species = factor(Species, species_label(species_ss)))
lp_ss <- lp_of_fits(fits, ss_data)

## Curve grid: each habitat over its observed range of one covariate (60 points), from a location-period table
curve_grid <- \(lp, var) lp %>%
  summarise(lo = min(.data[[var]]), hi = max(.data[[var]]), .by = any_of(c("Species", "Habitat"))) %>%
  mutate(x = map2(lo, hi, \(lo, hi) seq(lo, hi, length.out = 60))) %>%
  unnest(x) %>%
  select(-lo, -hi)
## Single-species curves (supplement): per species and habitat, from that species' fit
ss_curves <- \(beta_l, lp, var) curve_grid(lp, var) %>%
  mutate(draws = pmap(list(Species, Habitat, x), \(sp, h, x) pred_at(beta_l[[str_replace(sp, " ", "_")]], h, var, x))) %>%
  summarise_draws()
ssp_tbl <- ss_curves(ss_beta, lp_ss, "ssp")

## Community-level curves (main text, multi-species fits): within each posterior draw, the mean across the migrants of each species' predicted occupancy, as in the 98-species report; faint lines are each species' posterior median curve
ms_rain <- readRDS(fit_path("10_boreal_migrants", ms_rain_tag))
ms_rain_beta <- species_beta(ms_rain)

)

context_comm <- context_draws %>% mutate(draws = map(sp_draws, \(d) rowMeans(do.call(cbind, d)))) %>% select(-sp_draws) %>% summarise_draws()
context_species <- context_draws %>% mutate(Species = map(sp_draws, names), med = map(sp_draws, \(d) map_dbl(d, median))) %>% select(-sp_draws) %>% unnest(c(Species, med))
## Habitat use from the base multi-species model, community-level as above: occupancy in each habitat, and along silvopasture cover within 300 m averaged over the three habitats (equal weights); faint marks are each species' posterior medians
comm_hab_draws <- tibble(code = names(hab_labels), sp_draws = map(code, \(h) map(ms_beta, \(b) pred_occ(b, h)))) %>% mutate(Habitat = factor(hab_labels[code], hab_labels))

ssp_draws <- tibble(x = seq(min(lp_comm$ssp), max(lp_comm$ssp), length.out = 60)) %>% mutate(sp_draws = map(x, \(x) map(ms_beta, \(b) rowMeans(sapply(hab_labels, \(h) pred_at(b, h, "ssp", x))))))

## Community-level means of the species' rainfall slopes (logit scale, per SD) in the rainfall fit: forest, and silvopasture (forest slope plus silvopasture's difference)
comm_rain <- as.matrix(ms_rain$beta.comm.samples)

## Convergence of the rainfall fit: largest Rhat of the community-level means, and the among-species variances above 1.1
tau_rhat_rain <- set_names(ms_rain$rhat$tau.sq.beta, colnames(ms_rain$tau.sq.beta.samples))

## Single-species curves along one covariate, one panel per species, with location-period ticks coloured by habitat: along the top those where the species was detected, along the bottom those where it was not
ss_plot <- function(curves, lp, var, x_lab, edge = FALSE) {
  p <- ggplot(curves, aes(x, med, color = Habitat, fill = Habitat))
  if (edge) p <- p + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50")
  p + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl), alpha = 0.12, color = NA) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
    geom_rug(data = filter(lp, det), aes(x = .data[[var]], color = Habitat), sides = "t", alpha = 0.7, length = unit(0.05, "npc"), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    geom_rug(data = filter(lp, !det), aes(x = .data[[var]], color = Habitat), sides = "b", alpha = 0.4, length = unit(0.05, "npc"), inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    facet_wrap(~ Species, nrow = 1) +
    scale_color_manual(values = hab_colors, aesthetics = c("color", "fill")) +
    labs(x = x_lab, y = "Occupancy (use) probability") +
    theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "top", legend.box = "vertical", legend.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0), strip.text = element_text(face = "italic"))
}
```

## Abstract

**Goal:** To understand the impact of silvopasture on the community of Nearctic-Neotropical migrants.

**Motivation:** The multi-species model pools 98 species, so each species' habitat response is pulled toward the community mean, which makes the response of Nearctic-Neotropical migrants harder to determine. The functional trait models (Fig 7, preliminary results report) show that long-distance migrants' response to silvopasture relative to pasture trends more positive than that of resident species, but with wide uncertainty. Models geared specifically towards migrants allow for more tailored specification, as well as only including surveys conducted during the non-breeding season.

**Methods:** Here we fit a multi-species occupancy model for the community of Nearctic-Neotropical migrants, as well as single-species models for three species (*Setophaga striata, Setophaga ruticilla*, *Piranga rubra*), asking whether (1) silvopastural systems influence occupancy (relative pasture and forest fragments), (2) whether occupancy changes with rainfall, distance to the forest edge, or landscape forest cover, and (3) at what scale, if any, migrants respond to woody canopy cover in the surrounding landscape.

**Results:** The community of Nearctic-Neotropical migrants used silvopasture more than pasture, but tended to use it less than forest. Use was highest at the forest edge, declining both with distance into the open and with depth into forest, and there was moderate evidence that it rose with silvopasture cover within 300 m. Its response to annual rainfall did not clearly differ between silvopasture and forest. Results from the single-species models largely mirrored the multi-species model, which is not surprising given that these three species account for most detections, and nearly all the detections outside of forest: *S. ruticilla* also used silvopasture more than pasture, while *P. rubra*'s habitat contrasts were uncertain. *S. striata*, the most commonly detected migrant in our study, responded most strongly to silvopasture, using it more than both pasture and forest. It was also the only species with a clear landscape scale effect: its use declined with woody canopy cover within `r ring_km(striata_radius)`. For the community, canopy cover within `r ring_km(comm_radius)` improved model fit because species responded in opposite directions (e.g., *S. striata* negatively, *Catharus ustulatus* positively).

**Conclusions:** Our findings suggest that the community of Nearctic-Neotropical migrants would benefit from converting pasture to silvopasture, although for the average migrant silvopasture does not replace forest. Our findings for *S. striata* coincide with those of Morales-Rozo et al. (2025), who found higher occupancy in agroforestry systems (shade-grown cacao, citrus, silvopasture) than in native forest, and lower occupancy with more forest at the landscape scale.

{{< pagebreak >}}

## Methods

### Survey data

We used point counts conducted between `r comm_season_start_date`, the first migrant detection at our survey locations, and `r season_end_date`, the end of the non-breeding season in our data (Meta has no April surveys). Each point count location was visited repeatedly within a survey period, and we refer to a location surveyed in one period as a point count. The data comprise `r comm_n_visits` visits at `r comm_n_locations` locations in `r length(Periods_kept)` survey periods (`r period_text`), giving `r comm_lp_by_habitat[["Bosque"]]` forest, `r comm_lp_by_habitat[["Ssp"]]` silvopasture and `r comm_lp_by_habitat[["Pastizales"]]` pasture point counts on `r comm_farms_by_habitat[["Bosque"]]`, `r comm_farms_by_habitat[["Ssp"]]` and `r comm_farms_by_habitat[["Pastizales"]]` farms, respectively. Point counts received a median of `r median(comm_lp_visits)` visits, and the first and last visits were a median of `r median(comm_lp_span)` days apart (maximum `r max(comm_lp_span)` days). The 2016-17 surveys were almost entirely in forest, so the silvopasture and pasture data come from 2019 and 2026.

### Multi-species occupancy model

We fit a multi-season, multi-species spatial occupancy model (`spOccupancy::svcTMsPGOcc`) to the `r length(Migrants)` Nearctic-Neotropical migrants with at least 2 detections (@tbl-data), with Bernoulli occupancy and detection and logit links. Each species' coefficients were drawn from a community-level normal distribution, whose mean describes the average migrant and whose variance (inverse-gamma(1, 1) prior) sets how strongly species are pulled toward that mean.

Occupancy was modelled as a function of the predominant habitat within the 50-m point-count radius (forest as the reference level), annual rainfall, distance to the forest edge, silvopasture cover within 300 m, woody canopy cover within `r ring_km(comm_radius)` ([Scale of effect of landscape canopy cover](#sec-scale-methods)), and survey period (the two 2016-17 periods sharing one intercept). Detection was modelled as a function of whether the point was in forest, the start time of the count and its square, and the collector team, with a team-specific slope of log sampling day that lets each team's detection improve over its first days in the field.

To allow for differences in migratory schedule among species, we also included two timing indicators, assigned by the mean survey date of each point count. Point counts before `r comm_arrival_end_date` were considered arrival surveys, and those before `r passage_end_date` were also coded as passage surveys, leaving point counts from `r comm_arrival_end_date` to `r season_end_date` (the stationary wintering period) as the reference. Passage surveys made up `r passage_lp[["Ssp"]]` of the `r comm_lp_by_habitat[["Ssp"]]` silvopasture point counts, `r passage_lp[["Bosque"]]` of the `r comm_lp_by_habitat[["Bosque"]]` forest and `r passage_lp[["Pastizales"]]` of the `r comm_lp_by_habitat[["Pastizales"]]` pasture point counts. The arrival coefficient therefore contrasts arrival with stationary wintering, and the passage coefficient accounts for any additional flux of migrants during passage. This allows the passage detections of early migrants (e.g., *C. ustulatus*, `r passage_detections[["Catharus_ustulatus"]]` of its `r detections[["Catharus_ustulatus"]]` detections) to be modelled fully while leaving the estimates for late migrants largely unchanged. For example, compared with the same model fit from `r passage_end_date`, no habitat contrast of *S. striata* (which was never detected during passage) moved by more than `r sprintf("%.2f", passage_shift[["striata"]])` on the logit scale, and no community-level mean contrast by more than `r sprintf("%.2f", passage_shift[["comm"]])`.

A single spatial factor captured residual spatial structure shared among species, modelled as a nearest-neighbour Gaussian process (5 neighbours) with an exponential correlation function and a uniform prior on the effective range between `r free_range_km[1]` and `r free_range_km[2]` km, the largest distance between locations. The estimated effective range was short but uncertain, with a long upper tail (posterior median `r sprintf("%.1f", median(eff_range_km))` km, mean `r sprintf("%.1f", mean(eff_range_km))` km, 95% CrI `r sprintf("%.1f", quantile(eff_range_km, 0.025))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", quantile(eff_range_km, 0.975))` km). We ran `r Mcmc_long$n.chains` chains of `r format(n_iter_long, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` iterations (`r format(Mcmc_long$n.burn, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` burn-in, thinned by `r Mcmc_long$n.thin`). The largest community-level Rhat was `r sprintf("%.2f", max_rhat_comm)`, for the among-species variance of a collector team's warm-up slope, and `r sprintf("%.2f", max_rhat_comm_occ)` among the occupancy terms; `r if (n_sp_rhat == 0) "no" else n_sp_rhat` species coefficients had Rhat above 1.1.

### Single-species models

Because each species' estimates in the multi-species model are partially pooled toward the community-level mean, we checked the habitat-use results with single-species versions of the same model (`spOccupancy::stPGOcc`), each with its own spatial random effect, for the three migrants detected often enough outside forest to estimate habitat contrasts (*S. striata*, *S. ruticilla* and *P. rubra*). These models were additive, with forest again as the reference level, and included canopy cover only for *S. striata* (within `r ring_km(striata_radius)`), as no radius improved the *S. ruticilla* or *P. rubra* models.

Each species had its own survey window concordant with its migration ecology. *S. ruticilla* and *P. rubra* start on `r data_summary$Setophaga_ruticilla$start`, as in the multi-species model, whereas *S. striata* starts on `r data_summary$Setophaga_striata$start`, as it was not detected in the `r n_visits_before_first` visits from `r early_2019_dates` 2019 (first autumn detection on `r first_detection`). Each window ends at the end of the species' non-breeding season according to eBird Status and Trends (*S. striata* `r data_summary$Setophaga_striata$end`, *S. ruticilla* `r data_summary$Setophaga_ruticilla$end`, *P. rubra* `r data_summary$Piranga_rubra$end`), so that March visits after a species has left are not treated as non-use. An arrival indicator variable, from the survey start date to the start of its stationary non-breeding season (`r data_summary$Setophaga_striata$arrival_end`, `r data_summary$Setophaga_ruticilla$arrival_end` and `r data_summary$Piranga_rubra$arrival_end`, respectively), accounts for changes in migrant occupancy as birds are arriving on the wintering grounds. This leaves `r data_summary$Setophaga_striata$n_visits` visits at `r data_summary$Setophaga_striata$n_locations` locations for *S. striata*, `r data_summary$Setophaga_ruticilla$n_visits` at `r data_summary$Setophaga_ruticilla$n_locations` for *S. ruticilla* and `r data_summary$Piranga_rubra$n_visits` at `r data_summary$Piranga_rubra$n_locations` for *P. rubra*.

Few pasture point counts had a detection of any of the three species (@tbl-data), so pasture occupancy is weakly identified. As a sensitivity check, we refit *S. striata* models with pasture as the reference level (instead of forest), or with a different prior variance, to determine how that influenced our habitat contrasts. The direction of every silvopasture contrast remained unchanged, but the size of the contrast against pasture depended on these choices (`r sens_ref`). We did not run these checks for *S. ruticilla* and *P. rubra*, whose pasture estimates rest on even fewer detections and are likely at least as sensitive. Each model ran `r Mcmc$n.chains` chains of `r format(n_iter, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` iterations (`r format(Mcmc$n.burn, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` burn-in, thinned by `r Mcmc$n.thin`), and the largest Rhat across all parameters of the three fits was `r sprintf("%.2f", max_rhat_ss)`.

### Habitat-specific response to rainfall

The models above are additive, so all habitats share one slope for each covariate. To ask whether migrants respond to rainfall differently in silvopasture and forest, we fit a further multi-species model with a habitat-by-rainfall interaction and without pasture, which has too few detections to support its own slope. Rainfall varies only between farms, but the `r comm_season_start_date` season, whose passage surveys add farms, includes `r comm_nopast_farms[["Ssp"]]` silvopasture and `r comm_nopast_farms[["Bosque"]]` forest farms. In this model the community-level means converged (largest Rhat `r sprintf("%.2f", rain_rhat_means)`), but the among-species variances of `r paste0(names(rain_rhat_high), " (Rhat ", sprintf("%.2f", rain_rhat_high), ")", collapse = " and ")` mixed poorly; neither involves rainfall.

### Scale of effect of landscape canopy cover {#sec-scale-methods}

To find the scale at which migrants respond to landscape tree cover, we added woody canopy cover (survey-year maps) in a ring around each point to the additive models, one fit per outer radius: the `r length(Ring_radii_m) - 1` radii of the 98-species scale-of-effect analysis (`r min(Ring_radii_m)` m to 10 km) and 20 km, since migrants may perceive the landscape at large scales. Rings exclude the inner 50 m so that they do not duplicate the point's own habitat, and each radius was standardised over the `r nrow(Stacked_oc)` surveyed point counts of the 98-species data. We compared each fit by WAIC with the same model without canopy.

### Inference

We report the posterior median followed by the 95% credible interval (CrI) and, in the text, the posterior probability that the quantity is positive, e.g. `r est(ss_contrasts$Setophaga_striata[["Silvopasture vs pasture"]])` for *S. striata*'s silvopasture vs pasture contrast on the logit scale. We treat P(\>0) of at least 0.95 (or at most 0.05) as support for an effect and 0.80–0.95 (or 0.05–0.20) as moderate evidence, and describe weaker effects as trends.

## Results

### Habitat use

```{r}
#| label: tbl-data
#| tbl-cap: !expr data_cap
report_table(data_tbl, c("Species", "Visits with\na detection", "Point counts with a detection\n(pasture / silvopasture / forest)"), align = "lcc", widths = c("4cm", NA, NA))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-comm-habitat
#| fig-cap: !expr comm_habitat_cap
#| fig-height: 3.2
p_habitat <- ggplot(comm_by_habitat, aes(Habitat, med, color = Habitat)) +
  geom_point(data = species_by_habitat, position = position_jitter(width = 0.15, height = 0, seed = 1), alpha = 0.4, size = 1) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl), size = 0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = hab_colors, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Occupancy (use) probability", tag = "(a)") +
  theme_bw()
p_cover <- ggplot(comm_ssp_curve, aes(x, med)) +
  geom_line(data = species_ssp_curve, aes(group = Species), linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl), alpha = 0.15) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Silvopasture within 300 m (%)", y = NULL, tag = "(b)") +
  theme_bw() + theme(plot.margin = margin(5.5, 12, 5.5, 5.5))
patchwork::wrap_plots(p_habitat, p_cover, nrow = 1)
```

The average Nearctic-Neotropical migrant used silvopasture more than pasture (community-level mean contrast `r est(comm_contrasts[["Silvopasture vs pasture"]])`) but not more than forest (`r est(comm_contrasts[["Silvopasture vs forest"]])`; @fig-comm-habitat a), and there was moderate evidence that use rose with silvopasture cover within 300 m (community-level mean slope per SD of cover, `r round(ssp_scale$SD)` percentage points, `r est(comm_beta[, "ssp"])`; @fig-comm-habitat b). Six of the ten species had at most `r max(detections[rare_sp])` detections, and their pasture coefficients barely departed from the community-level mean (each within `r sprintf("%.1f", max(abs(rare_dev_pasture)))` on the logit scale), so the data say little about how these species use pasture. Their silvopasture coefficients varied more, from `r sprintf("%.1f", min(rare_dev_ssp))` to `r sprintf("%+.1f", max(rare_dev_ssp))` around the community-level mean. Of these six, *`r species_label(rare_top)`* leaned most toward silvopasture (silvopasture vs forest `r est(ms_contrasts[[rare_top]][["Silvopasture vs forest"]])`), though `r passage_detections[[rare_top]]` of its `r detections[[rare_top]]` detections came during passage.

The single-species models largely agreed with the multi-species model (@fig-habitat). *S. striata* stood out from the community by using silvopasture more than both pasture (`r ss_c("Setophaga_striata", "Silvopasture vs pasture")`) and forest (`r ss_c("Setophaga_striata", "Silvopasture vs forest")`), in line with Morales-Rozo et al. (2025). *S. ruticilla* also used silvopasture more than pasture (`r ss_c("Setophaga_ruticilla", "Silvopasture vs pasture")`), with moderate evidence that it used forest more than silvopasture (`r ss_c("Setophaga_ruticilla", "Silvopasture vs forest")`). *P. rubra*'s habitat contrasts were uncertain due to low sample sizes. In the single-species models, use rose with silvopasture cover within 300 m for *P. rubra* (`r ss_b("Piranga_rubra", "ssp")`) and *S. striata* (`r ss_b("Setophaga_striata", "ssp")`), with moderate evidence for *S. ruticilla* (`r ss_b("Setophaga_ruticilla", "ssp")`) (@fig-ssp).

### Landscape context

```{r}
#| label: fig-context
#| fig-cap: !expr context_cap
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(context_comm, aes(x, med, color = Habitat, fill = Habitat)) +
  geom_vline(data = tibble(Panel = factor(context_specs$Panel[2], context_specs$Panel)), aes(xintercept = 0), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(data = context_species, aes(group = interaction(Species, Habitat)), linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lcl, ymax = ucl), alpha = 0.15, color = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ Panel, scales = "free_x", strip.position = "bottom", labeller = label_wrap_gen(22)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = hab_colors, aesthetics = c("color", "fill")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Occupancy (use) probability", color = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "top", strip.placement = "outside", strip.background = element_blank())
```

The average migrant's response to rainfall did not clearly differ between silvopasture and forest (@fig-context a): the community-level mean rainfall slope in silvopasture differed from that in forest by `r est(comm_rain[, "Habitat_frefSsp:Tot_prec"])` (logit scale, per SD of annual rainfall, `r round(prec_scale$SD)` mm). In the additive single-species models, habitat use rose with rainfall for all three species (P(\>0) = `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(ss_beta$Setophaga_striata[, "Tot_prec"] > 0))` for *S. striata*, `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(ss_beta$Setophaga_ruticilla[, "Tot_prec"] > 0))` for *S. ruticilla* and `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(ss_beta$Piranga_rubra[, "Tot_prec"] > 0))` for *P. rubra*).

The average migrant's use was highest at the forest edge (@fig-context b), with support for a decline on both sides: the community-level mean slope per SD of distance (`r round(dist_sd_m)` m) was `r est(comm_beta[, "Dist_open"])` into the open (pasture and silvopasture) and `r est(comm_beta[, "Dist_inside"])` inside forest.

### Scale of effect of landscape canopy cover {#sec-scale}

```{r}
#| label: fig-ring
#| fig-cap: !expr ring_cap
#| fig-height: 5.5
ring %>%
  filter(!is.na(Radius_m), Chains == "short") %>%
  pivot_longer(c(dWAIC, Canopy_median), names_to = "name", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(lo = if_else(name == "dWAIC", NA_real_, Canopy_lo), hi = if_else(name == "dWAIC", NA_real_, Canopy_hi),
         name = recode(name, dWAIC = "WAIC minus WAIC without canopy", Canopy_median = "Canopy coefficient (logit, per 10 percentage points)"),
         Species = str_replace(Species, "_", " "), Model = if_else(Species == "Community", "Multi-species", "Single-species"), name = fct_relevel(name, "WAIC minus WAIC without canopy")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Radius_m / 1000, y = value, colour = Species)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.08), na.rm = TRUE, size = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = Model), position = position_dodge(width = 0.08)) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(`Multi-species` = "solid", `Single-species` = "dashed"), guide = "none") +
  # Community in black so it stands apart from the species; species colours avoid the habitat palette of the other figures
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Community = "black", `Piranga rubra` = "#0072B2", `Setophaga ruticilla` = "#D55E00", `Setophaga striata` = "#CC79A7"), labels = \(x) parse(text = if_else(x == "Community", x, paste0("italic('", x, "')")))) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ name, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Outer ring radius (km)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

For the community, WAIC improved most at `r ring_km(ring_best("Community")$Radius_m)` (ΔWAIC `r ring_dw("Community", comm_radius)`), with 2 and 5 km close behind. Use changed little with canopy cover for the average migrant (community-level mean `r est(ms_ring_sp_comm)` per 10 percentage points; @fig-context c), but the among-species SD of the canopy coefficient was large (`r ci(ms_ring_tau_sd)`), suggesting that species respond to landscape forest cover in different directions rather than in a shared way. For example, *S. striata* (`r est(ms_ring_sp$Setophaga_striata)`) and *C. ustulatus* (`r est(ms_ring_sp$Catharus_ustulatus)`) responded in opposite directions, and the six rarely detected species leaned negative with wide intervals.

Among the single-species models, only *S. striata* showed a clear scale of effect (@fig-ring): WAIC fell smoothly from 1 km to a minimum at `r ring_km(ring_best("Setophaga_striata")$Radius_m)` (ΔWAIC `r ring_dw("Setophaga_striata", striata_radius)`) and rose again beyond 7.5 km. In its base model (full-length chains), use declined with canopy cover within `r ring_km(striata_radius)` (`r est(striata_canopy)` per 10 percentage points; ΔWAIC `r sprintf("%.1f", striata_dwaic)` against the same model without canopy), consistent with the negative relationship with forest cover within 1 km found by Morales-Rozo et al. (2025). For *S. ruticilla*, no radius up to 10 km changed WAIC by more than `r sprintf("%.0f", max(abs(filter(ring, Species == "Setophaga_ruticilla", Chains == "short", Radius_m <= 10000)$dWAIC)))`, and only the 20 km ring improved it (ΔWAIC `r ring_dw("Setophaga_ruticilla", 20000)`, canopy `r ring_est(ring_row("Setophaga_ruticilla", 20000))`). This may reflect a true but weak response at broad scales, but the overlap among rings of 20 km or more leaves too little contrast to test such scales in this dataset. *P. rubra*'s profile was flat within run-to-run MCMC noise (ΔWAIC `r sprintf("%.1f", min(filter(ring, Species == "Piranga_rubra", Chains == "short")$dWAIC))` at best), with positive but unclear coefficients.

### Nearctic-Neotropical migrants outside Meta

Extending the models to other regions would add few detections outside forest. Within the same season window, the other ecoregions have `r out_effort[["Ssp"]]` silvopasture and `r out_effort[["Pastizales"]]` pasture visits, against `r out_effort[["Bosque"]]` in forest, and `r out_forest[["forest"]]` of the `r out_forest[["all"]]` visits with a Nearctic-Neotropical migrant outside Meta were in forest (@tbl-outside; survey effort in @tbl-effort). The main gains would be *Setophaga fusca*, an Andean winterer detected mostly in Eje Cafetero forest; *Setophaga petechia*, detected in both forest and silvopasture; and more forest data for *P. rubra* and *C. ustulatus*.

## Next steps

- Check the season window against eBird arrival and departure dates in Meta.
- Test closure: does detection on a visit depend on the days since the previous visit to the same point count?
- Season-specific rainfall from CHIRPS (Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data; free, daily to monthly, about 5 km resolution) to test whether *S. striata* shifts habitat in drier years.

## Collaborator questions

**Occupancy or use?** Wintering migrants may move among points between visits. If they do, closure is violated: occupancy then estimates the probability that a location was *used* during the survey period, and detection estimates availability times detectability (Rota et al. 2009). The first and last visits to a point count were a median of `r median(comm_lp_span)` days apart (maximum `r max(comm_lp_span)` days), which limits movement between visits, so closure may hold well enough to read the estimates as occupancy. I currently call them occupancy (use); should we instead treat them as occupancy proper, or keep the more cautious reading?
